analysis.one_liner: Sets national patient-protection rules for managed care plans: outside appeals of denials, guaranteed emergency coverage, and plan disclosure.
analysis.headline: This bipartisan managed-care patient-protection bill never got a Senate committee vote or floor vote; it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required health plans and insurers to give patients timely coverage decisions, internal and independent external appeals of denials, and written reasons when care is denied. It would have covered emergency care without prior approval, let women see OB/GYNs without referrals, required hospital stays after mastectomies, banned gag rules on doctors, and forced plans to disclose what they cover and how they pay providers. The Senate health committee never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in managed care plans and employer health coverage — tens of millions of Americans — who currently face denial of care with limited recourse. The bill would have given them independent external review of denials, binding on the plan, emergency care without pre-approval under a 'prudent layperson' standard, direct access to OB/GYN and pediatric care, guaranteed hospital stays for breast cancer surgery, doctors free to discuss all treatment options, and a federally funded ombudsman to help patients navigate grievances.

how_it_helps.text: Patients whose coverage is denied could take the case to an independent external review entity with no financial tie to the plan; the entity's decision would be final and binding on the plan, and the plan would pay the review's costs [S3].

Plans would have to cover emergency services without prior authorization, whether or not the provider is in-network, and patients could not be billed more than in-network cost-sharing for emergency care — with 'emergency' defined by what a prudent layperson would believe, not what the plan says after the fact [S3].

Plans could not penalize doctors for advocating for their patients or for providing information and referrals for medical care, and could not interfere with the treating physician's decisions about medically necessary care [S2].

Patients would get timely coverage determinations (72 hours in urgent cases), written reasons for denials in plain language, and coverage of an appropriate hospital stay after mastectomies and lymph node dissections [S2, S3].

The bill would fund independent Health Insurance Ombudsmen in every state to counsel patients and help with grievances and appeals, and require plans to publicly report quality data so consumers can compare them [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health plans, health insurers, and self-insured employers, who would bear the cost of new appeals infrastructure, external reviews, expanded coverage requirements, and liability for economic losses caused by untimely or improper coverage decisions. Some of that cost would likely be passed on in premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose significant new administrative requirements on every plan and insurer — utilization review rules, grievance and appeal procedures, disclosure of detailed plan information, and quality reporting — compliance costs that would likely show up in premiums [S2].

It would make any person responsible for a coverage decision that is untimely or not made in accordance with plan terms liable to the patient for economic loss, expanding legal exposure for plans and employers beyond what existed under ERISA's limits on lawsuits [S2].

Despite its name as a patient bill of rights, the bill preserves ERISA's preemption of state law for group health plans (Sec. 3) and stops well short of the broad right to sue in court for denied or improper care that other patient-protection proposals of the era included, so its enforcement against plans was comparatively limited [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing denied or delayed care, the external appeals process, binding decisions, and guaranteed emergency coverage would have addressed real, documented harms of 1990s managed care. The honest cost is real: new compliance and review obligations, plus liability for untimely decisions, would raise plan administration costs and probably premiums, and the bill's own design preserved ERISA preemption, making its remedies narrower than the full right-to-sue versions debated at the time. On balance it was a moderate compromise: meaningful protections at a deliberately limited cost, which is why it drew both Republican and Democratic cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with bipartisan cosponsors and sent to the Senate health committee, which never took it up; it died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Chafee (R-RI) introduced the bill on February 4, 1999, joined by seven cosponsors — five Democrats and two Republicans [S1, S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearings recorded, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care insurers and self-insured employers came out ahead: they avoided the external-review obligation, the emergency-care and mastectomy-stay mandates, and the new liability for untimely coverage decisions. Patients with denied claims were left to rely on whatever protections state law provided — which, because of ERISA preemption, covered only a portion of the insured population.

sides.party_line_note: The bill itself was bipartisan — a Republican lead sponsor with 7 cosponsors split 5 Democrats and 2 Republicans — and died quietly in committee rather than on a party-line vote; the wider patient-protection fight of 1999–2001, however, split largely along party lines over how far to let patients sue.

industries.industry: Managed care plans and health insurers
industries.note: The bill would have forced plans to pay for binding independent external reviews, cover out-of-network emergency care at in-network rates, guarantee post-mastectomy stays, and stop tying doctor pay to denying care. Insurers would lose discretion over coverage denials that patients currently cannot override — their interest in the bill ran directly against patients seeking care.

The bill would have applied the same patient protections to the roughly half of insured workers covered by self-insured employer plans, which are otherwise largely exempt from state insurance rules, and exposed plan fiduciaries to penalties and liability for bad faith. Employers would bear these costs, though their interest aligned with the bill's limits on lawsuits rather than the right-to-sue versions.

The bill would ban gag clauses, prohibit plans from penalizing doctors who advocate for patients or help with appeals, and restrict physician incentive plans that reward withholding care. Doctors would also benefit from independent review overriding plan denials.

Prudent-layperson emergency coverage without prior authorization, and payment rules protecting patients from excess out-of-network emergency charges, would reduce coverage disputes and uncompensated care disputes over emergency visits.
